# HMS Hyperion (1807)

HMS Hyperion was a frigate of the British Royal Navy, representing the quintessential warship of the late 18th and early 19th centuries , . Launched in 1807, she was a fifth-rate vessel, a classification denoting a medium-sized warship typically carrying between 20 and 50 guns . The ship served as a workhorse of the fleet throughout the tumultuous period of the Napoleonic Wars and beyond, participating in numerous actions against French and allied vessels. Her career spanned over two decades, demonstrating both her durability and the Royal Navy's reliance on such well-designed warships. Despite extensive archival records confirming her active service far into the 1820s, a significant point of uncertainty remains regarding her ultimate fate, with some historical accounts suggesting an early demise that is contradicted by more contemporary and detailed personnel records. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of HMS Hyperion (1807), drawing upon authoritative secondary histories and primary archival sources to reconstruct her design, construction, service history, command structure, and final disposition.

## Design and Construction

The genesis of HMS Hyperion lies in the ongoing evolution of Royal Navy frigate design, a process heavily influenced by the need to counter the formidable French frigates of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic eras . She belonged to a class of 32-gun fifth-rate frigates designed by John Henslow, who served as Surveyor of the Navy from 1787 to 1805 , . Henslow’s designs were renowned for their balance of speed, firepower, and seaworthiness, often incorporating elements learned from captured enemy vessels. Specifically, the design of HMS Hyperion was based on the lines of the French frigate *Magicienne*, a 36-gun vessel of 1778, which provided a proven and effective hull form that British designers adapted for their own needs . This lineage placed her within a cohort of highly capable ships, including contemporaries like HMS Bucephalus (launched 1808) and HMS Pyramus (launched 1810), all of which were products of the same design philosophy aimed at achieving superiority in single-ship actions , .

Details concerning her physical construction present a degree of ambiguity, reflecting the fragmented nature of some historical records. One source attributes her construction to Edward Hunt at Chatham Dockyard . However, another, more specific piece of evidence points to a different origin. A signed original ship plan for HMS Hyperion, created by Edward Churchill, Master Shipwright at Plymouth Dockyard, exists in the collection of the National Maritime Museum . This document, held under reference J0416, provides a detailed front and side elevation of the vessel, offering a visual testament to her construction and design at that specific dockyard . The discrepancy between these two claims highlights the importance of consulting multiple primary sources; while one account may attribute construction to a particular yard, official plans might bear the signature of the master shipwright responsible for overseeing the build. The lack of her name appearing in the index to the Navy Board Progress Books, which list building and repair costs, suggests that dockyard records for this period may be incomplete or imprecise, further complicating a definitive reconstruction of her construction timeline .

Her dimensions were substantial for a fifth-rate frigate. The ship measured 150 feet along the gun deck, a standard length for a 32-gun vessel of her class, providing ample space for her crew and armament . While her official classification was as a 32-gun frigate, her actual armament appears to have been configured differently. According to one detailed source, her battery consisted of 28 x 18-pounder long guns mounted on the main deck, supplemented by 2 x 9-pounder guns on the quarterdeck . This configuration was augmented by 10 x 32-pounder carronades, powerful short-range weapons ideal for close-quarters combat, which were typical additions to British frigates of the era , . Rif Winfield, in his definitive work on the subject, corroborates the use of '32pdr carronades' on Hyperion, reinforcing the mix of long-range broadsides and devastating close-range firepower that characterized her design . The complement of the ship was recorded as 640 men, a figure that seems exceptionally high for a 32-gun frigate, which typically carried crews in the range of 250-400 men. Such a large number could suggest an unusually heavy complement for wartime operations or may reflect an administrative total rather than a typical sailing complement. The only surviving official muster rolls would provide the definitive answer to this question , . Her launch date is firmly established as 1807, placing her squarely within the peak of Britain's naval expansion during the Napoleonic Wars , .

## Service History

The service history of HMS Hyperion is one of remarkable longevity and continuous activity, extending far beyond the conclusion of the Napoleonic Wars. Following her launch in 1807, she was swiftly integrated into the Royal Navy's fleet, serving on various stations where she engaged in the critical mission of countering French maritime power . Contemporary records, such as the List of H.M. Navy corrected to 1809, confirm her active status within the navy by that year, solidifying her presence as a working warship in the immediate post-launch period . Her operational life was not confined to a single theater but encompassed diverse duties across the globe. Historical accounts indicate that she served on the Mediterranean Station, a key area of conflict during the Napoleonic Wars where the Royal Navy sought to blockade French ports and protect British interests . This deployment underscores her versatility and the strategic importance assigned to her by the Admiralty.

One of the most significant documented actions involving HMS Hyperion was the capture of the privateer Rattlesnake , . Privateers were privately owned vessels authorized by their governments to attack enemy shipping, and they posed a significant threat to British merchant convoys and naval supply lines. The capture of such a vessel demonstrates Hyperion's role in protecting commerce and asserting British naval supremacy. The chronology of this event is particularly important; a seaman's service record confirms he was serving aboard the ship from March 1811 until June 1812 . This directly corroborates the timing of the action, placing it firmly within her active service period and refuting any notion of a premature end to her career. This engagement aligns perfectly with the broader operational context of the era, where frigates like Hyperion were frequently tasked with hunting down and destroying these elusive raiders in the English Channel, the Bay of Biscay, and the Atlantic approaches .

The narrative of her service is marked by a striking contradiction regarding a famous exploit attributed to her. An account claims that in July 1800, Hyperion led a squadron of small craft to attack four blockaded French frigates off Boulogne, successfully capturing one . However, this claim is historically impossible given that the ship in question, launched in 1807, simply did not exist in 1800. This event must be considered a misattribution, likely conflating the identity of this vessel with another ship named *Hyperion* that may have served earlier or with a similarly named ship altogether. This highlights the necessity of rigorous cross-referencing of all historical accounts against a strict chronological framework derived from primary sources. Despite this error, the body of verifiable evidence paints a picture of a durable and active warship. Her career extended well past the Battle of Trafalgar and the initial conclusion of hostilities with France. Multiple entries in Royal Navy pay books prove she remained in commission and actively manned for many years after the end of the Napoleonic Wars , . Records show an Able Seaman serving aboard her pay book from September 1829 to December 1829, and another from March 1829 to April 1829, confirming her continued service at least until late 1829 , . Another pay book entry shows a crew member serving from June 1828 to February 1831, though this may refer to a different vessel also named HMS Hyperion, a separate ship launched in 1825 . Regardless, the evidence overwhelmingly supports the conclusion that the 1807 Hyperion had a long and distinguished career, serving as a vital asset to the Royal Navy for over two decades.

## Commanding Officers

A definitive and complete list of all commanding officers who served aboard HMS Hyperion (1807) requires direct consultation of primary archival records, specifically the series of commissioned officer service records known as ADM 196, held at The National Archives , . These records are the most reliable source for identifying officers who held command or served in senior positions on a ship, detailing their names, ranks, dates of commission, postings, and periods of service , . By searching the indexes for ADM 196, covering the period 1756–1917, it would be possible to construct a precise chronology of command for the entire lifespan of HMS Hyperion . Each entry in these records typically lists the ships served on, the ranks held during each posting, and promotions, providing a granular view of an officer's career trajectory . For example, a record for Sir Fleetwood Broughton Reynolds Pellew meticulously documents his service on various vessels, including flag-hoisting and flag-lowering orders, offering a template for the level of detail available for commanders of HMS Hyperion .

In addition to the ADM 196 series, other collections of records can supplement the search for information on the ship's commanders. Full and half pay registers for commissioned officers, found in the ADM 22–25 and PMG 15 series, may contain commission dates and postings relevant to identifying commanding officers . Furthermore, the ADM 12 series, which contains indexes to letters received by the Admiralty concerning specific ships, can provide digests of correspondence that might mention appointments or removals of captains . The captains' logs themselves, held in the ADM 51 series, are invaluable as they often begin with the appointment of the new commander, thereby linking the logbook volume directly to a specific individual's command , . Finally, the Navy Board Progress Books (ADM 180), which list building and fitting costs, sometimes include survey information that could provide clues about the ship's state when first commissioned, potentially linking it to a particular captain's tenure .

The initial commanding officer of HMS Hyperion upon her commissioning in 1807 is not explicitly named in the provided sources. However, her presence in the List of H.M. Navy corrected to 1809 confirms she was fully operational by that time, meaning a commander must have taken charge shortly after her launch . The first confirmed commander mentioned in the materials is Thomas Brodie . The existence of his name in the ADM 196 indexes indicates that he served aboard the ship, and a deeper dive into the specific volumes would reveal the exact dates of his command . It is highly probable that Brodie was one of the early commanders of the vessel. The service history of the ship, spanning from 1807 to at least 1829, implies that she had several commanding officers over her long career , . Each change in command would represent a new chapter in her story, with different leaders shaping her performance in battle, discipline at sea, and overall operational effectiveness. Therefore, a comprehensive research effort focused on the aforementioned archival series is essential to populate the article with a complete and accurate list of her commanders, moving beyond the partial information currently available.

## Final Disposition

The final disposition of HMS Hyperion (1807) presents a clear case of conflicting historical narratives, where a modern anecdotal account is decisively refuted by a wealth of contemporary primary source documentation. The contradictory claim states that the ship was "wrecked near Newhaven on the west coast of Ireland in December 1811" . This assertion, if true, would mark a tragic and early end to her career, just four years after her launch. However, a thorough examination of official naval records reveals this date to be incorrect and places her in active service for many years thereafter. The most authoritative source on this matter is the Royal Navy Loss List, a free online database compiled by the Maritime Archaeology Sea Trust (MAST) that catalogs all Royal Navy warships lost in service since 1512 , . This database draws on official Admiralty records, memoirs, and archaeological reports to verify its findings . Crucially, HMS Hyperion is not listed among the vessels lost in 1807 or any other year prior to 1812 , . The absence of a ship from such a meticulously maintained list is itself strong negative evidence supporting her survival through 1811.

The most compelling evidence against the 1811 wreck claim comes from personal service records of sailors who served aboard the ship. These documents provide irrefutable proof of her continued commission. A detailed service record for an Able Seaman shows him serving aboard HMS Hyperion from 26 March 1811 to 18 August 1814 . His progression from Able Seaman to Ship's Corporal and finally Coxswain over this three-year period confirms he was not just a transient crew member but a part of the ship's permanent establishment during that time . It is physically impossible for such a record to exist if the ship had been lost in a wreck in December 1811. This single piece of evidence is sufficient to dismiss the earlier claim. Further corroboration is found in the ship's pay books. Entries from pay book number SB 3342 confirm an active crew serving aboard the ship between 18 September 1829 and 20 December 1829 . Another pay book entry shows an Able Seaman serving from 4 March 1829 to 26 April 1829 . These records definitively prove that HMS Hyperion remained in Royal Navy service, with a full crew and active administration, at least until mid-1829, over sixteen years after the claimed wreck date , .

Given this overwhelming evidence, the conclusion is inescapable: the claim of a 1811 wreck is erroneous. The most probable explanation for this historical error is a confusion of identities, perhaps conflating this vessel with another ship named *Hyperion* that may have served in the Boulogne area during the events described, or a general misattribution common in less-detailed historical accounts. The correct historical record indicates that HMS Hyperion (1807) had a long and distinguished career that lasted well into the post-Napoleonic era. She was decommissioned sometime after 1829. The exact circumstances of her decommissioning, disposal, or eventual sale are not detailed in the provided sources. This represents a gap in the known history of the vessel, a common outcome for many ships whose careers ended without a dramatic final act. Her legacy is therefore defined not by a sudden end but by a sustained period of dedicated service to the Royal Navy.

## Technical Specifications

The technical specifications of HMS Hyperion (1807) place her firmly within the standard profile of a Royal Navy fifth-rate frigate of the Napoleonic Wars era. As a 32-gun vessel, she was classified as a fifth-rate frigate, a designation that governed her size, crew complement, and armament , . These ships were the workhorses of the fleet, versatile enough for independent cruising, convoy escort, and participation in major fleet actions. The table below summarizes the verified technical data for HMS Hyperion, synthesized from authoritative secondary sources and primary documents.

| Attribute | Specification |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Ship Class** | Fifth Rate Frigate , |
| **Armament** | 28 × 18-pdr long guns, 2 × 9-pdr guns, 10 × 32-pdr carronades , |
| **Length** | 150 ft (gun deck measurement) |
| **Complement** | 640 men (recorded figure; typical complement for this class was 250-400) |
| **Builder / Yard** | Edward Hunt at Chatham Dockyard (per one source); Edward Churchill, Master Shipwright at Plymouth Dockyard (per ship plan) , |
| **Launched** | 1807 , |

The armament of HMS Hyperion reflects the tactical doctrines of the age. The primary battery of 28 x 18-pounder long guns on her main deck provided significant long-range firepower, allowing her to engage enemy ships effectively before closing to melee distances . The additional 2 x 9-pounder guns on the quarterdeck added flexibility, while the 10 x 32-pounder carronades represented the shift towards powerful, short-range weaponry ideal for the brutal, close-quarters fighting that often characterized frigate duels , . This mixed armament made her a formidable opponent in almost any engagement scenario. The stated complement of 640 men is a point of note and potential discrepancy. While a 32-gun frigate required a substantial crew, a figure of this magnitude is unusually high compared to typical complements for the class, which generally ranged from 250 to 400 men depending on the voyage and operational tempo . This higher number may reflect wartime conditions, an unusually large number of marines, or an administrative total rather than a typical sailing complement. The official muster rolls held in The National Archives (ADM 36 series) would be the only definitive source for verifying the actual crew numbers per muster period , .

The ship's design, based on the French frigate *Magicienne*, ensured she possessed the qualities necessary for a successful frigate: speed, maneuverability, and a robust hull . Her 150-foot gun deck length was characteristic of her class, providing a stable platform for her heavy guns while maintaining a relatively low silhouette . The existence of a signed ship plan by Edward Churchill at Plymouth Dockyard provides a rare glimpse into her precise construction and proportions . This document, now housed in the National Maritime Museum, serves as a crucial primary source for naval historians, offering details on her hull form and structural features that are not always apparent from textual descriptions alone . In summary, HMS Hyperion was a well-proportioned and heavily armed frigate, embodying the best practices of British naval architecture in the early 19th century. Her specifications made her a potent instrument of British naval power, suited for the demanding roles she undertook throughout her long and active service career.

[![Image 26: HMS Ardent sinking photo](https://defbrief.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Database-detailing-all-Royal-Navy-ship-losses-since-16th-century-now-available-online-640x491.jpg)](https://defbrief.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Database-detailing-all-Royal-Navy-ship-losses-since-16th-century-now-available-online.jpg)

Royal Navy file photo of HMS Ardent, which was sunk by Argentine aircraft in the Falkland Sound on 21 May 1982

**If you ever wondered how many ships and under which circumstances the Royal Navy lost since 1512, a new database that has become available to public is the best place to look.**

The [Royal Navy Loss List](https://thisismast.org//research/royal-navy-loss-list-search.html) is a free online database which lists 5,100 warships and auxiliaries lost in naval service since the days of Henry VIII.

Created by the Maritime Archaeology Sea Trust in 2011, it was originally intended to help legal and conservation experts protect Royal Navy wrecks around the globe.

They realized it would prove of use and interest to fellow historians and the wider public, and have made it accessible to all.

The database is searchable by a ship’s name, class, and tonnage. Or you can list the vessels lost in French waters over the past 500 years (760), the number of ships lost on D-Day (416), or how many were sunk by aircraft in the Great War (six).

The database draws on official records and a raft of reference works, plus memoirs and eyewitness accounts where necessary.

Archaeological reports, and diver accounts were used to verify information on the survival of vessel remains.

Even then, says Giles Richardson, MAST’s senior archaeologist, the cause of many losses remains a mystery; more than half the ships lost in World War 2 are classified ‘unknown – lost in action’ due to lack of information.

Many of these are landing craft and other small vessels lost in major operations including Dunkirk, and Operations Torch and Overlord, when official loss reports were only collated centrally months later, and eyewitnesses had long since moved on.

“Delving into contemporary accounts reveals craft officially recorded as simply as ‘lost’ on the Normandy beaches suffered a wide variety of fates, including storm damage, mechanical breakdown and collision.”

The list covers all vessels lost in peace and war – but not RAF, Army, Coastguard and merchant craft upon which RN personnel may have served, nor ships captured by the enemy or those lost in the service of other navies or converted to merchantmen.

The database offers some fascinating statistics about the fate of Royal Navy ships down the ages.

Of the 5,100 wrecks listed, more than a quarter – 1,410 – are in the UK’s territorial waters and another 156 are within the UK’s Exclusive Economic Zone, extending 200 nautical miles from the coast.

Until the turn of the 20th Century accidental shipwreck rather than battle were responsible for the vast majority of losses, whereas conflict accounts for three quarters of all RN/RFA ships sunk since 1900.

Mines destroyed one in every four ships sunk in both world wars. And while three in every 100 ships lost in the Great War fell victim to enemy aircraft, a generation later air power accounted for nearly one third of all the Royal Navy’s losses. In all, 300 vessels were lost to aircraft and 605 to submarines.

The database has been hailed as a vital resource – both for the casual viewer and the serious historian/marine archaeologist – by the National Museum of the Royal Navy.

“The RN Loss List is a vital tool to begin to understand, research and manage these 5,100 wreck sites before they are lost forever,” said its director general, Professor Dominic Tweddle.

“The United Kingdom has a huge, rich and astoundingly diverse underwater heritage from Bronze Age boats to World War 2 wrecks – and it is a heritage which is spread around the globe.

“The National Museum of the Royal Navy displays extraordinary objects which have come from some of these wrecks: the bells of HMS Hood and HMS Prince of Wales, everyday objects from HMS Stirling Castle lost in 1703 and the amazing cutwater of HMS Invincible lost in 1758.

“It is vital that these myriad wrecks are treated as seriously as archaeological sites on land and this fantastic loss list compiled by MAST represents a huge step forward.”

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

**Sir Henry Peake** (1753–1825) was a shipbuilder and designer to the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") who rose to be [Surveyor of the Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveyor_of_the_Navy "Surveyor of the Navy").

He was born in 1753 in (or close to) [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth "Portsmouth"). He joined the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") in May 1762 aged only 9, as an apprentice ship's carpenter. "Henry Peake" who is noted as Master Boat Builder at Portsmouth Dockyard in 1762 clearly cannot be the same person and this is probably his father. The Royal Navy list his works from 1779 when he became Master Shipwright at [Sheerness Dockyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheerness_Dockyard "Sheerness Dockyard").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-auto-1)

In June 1806 he replaced [Sir John Henslow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henslow_/(Surveyor_of_the_Navy/) "John Henslow (Surveyor of the Navy)") as [Surveyor of the Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveyor_of_the_Navy "Surveyor of the Navy"), working alongside [Sir William Rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rule_/(Surveyor_of_the_Navy/) "William Rule (Surveyor of the Navy)"). Hos position as [Surveyor of the Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveyor_of_the_Navy "Surveyor of the Navy") was filled by [Ropert Seppings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Robert_Seppings "Sir Robert Seppings") in 1813 but he did not officially retire until 1822.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-auto-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-2)

He was knighted by [the Prince Regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_George_IV "King George IV") on 25 June 1814. Peake died in 1825.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-auto-1)

He was married to Sarah Ladd. They had several sons who became eminent Royal Navy officers:[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-3)

*   Admiral [Thomas Ladd Peake](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Ladd_Peake&action=edit&redlink=1 "Thomas Ladd Peake (page does not exist)") (1782-1865)
*   Commander William Peake (1780-1813) killed on [HMS _Peacock_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Peacock_/(1806/) "HMS Peacock (1806)")
*   James Peake
*   Commander Henry Frederick Peake[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-4)

*   [HMS Polyphemus (1782)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Polyphemus_/(1782/) "HMS Polyphemus (1782)") 64-gun [ship of the line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_of_the_line "Ship of the line") launched at Sheerness
*   [HMS Europa (1783)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Europa_/(1783/) "HMS Europa (1783)") 50-gun ship of the line launched at Woolwich
*   [HMS Vanguard (1787)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Vanguard_/(1787/) "HMS Vanguard (1787)") 74-gun ship of the line launched at Deptford
*   [HMS Grampus (1802)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Grampus_/(1802/) "HMS Grampus (1802)") 50-gun ship of the line launched at Portsmouth
*   [HMS Colossus (1803)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Colossus_/(1803/) "HMS Colossus (1803)") 74-gun ship of the line launched at Deptford
*   Royal Sovereign (1804) unarmed yacht launched at Deptford
*   [HMS Hebe (1804)](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=HMS_Hebe_\(1804\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "HMS Hebe (1804) (page does not exist)") 32-gun [frigate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frigate "Frigate") launched at Deptford
*   [HMS Arrow (1805)](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=HMS_Arrow_\(1805\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "HMS Arrow (1805) (page does not exist)") 14-gun [schooner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schooner "Schooner") launched at Deptford
*   [HMS Minerva (1805)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Minerva_/(1805/) "HMS Minerva (1805)") 32-gun frigate launched at Deptford

Note: dates in brackets represent date of design not launch)

*   [HMS Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Brunswick_/(1790/) "HMS Brunswick (1790)") (1786) 74-gun ship of the line launched in 1790
*   [HMS Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=HMS_Bermuda_\(1808\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "HMS Bermuda (1808) (page does not exist)") (1806) 10-gun sloop
*   [Cherokee-class brig-sloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee-class_brig-sloop "Cherokee-class brig-sloop") (1807) a series of over one hundred 10-gun sloop
*   [HMS Rapid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Rapid "HMS Rapid") (1808) 16-gun sloop
*   [Pygmy-class schooner](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pygmy-class_schooner&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pygmy-class schooner (page does not exist)") (1809) 10-gun schooner
*   [Vesuvius-class sloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesuvius-class_sloop "Vesuvius-class sloop") (1812) 10-gun sloop equipped as a bomb vessel
*   [HMS Terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Terror_/(1813/) "HMS Terror (1813)") (1812)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-5) Vesuvius class bomb ship
*   [HMS Erebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Erebus_/(1826/) "HMS Erebus (1826)")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Peake#cite_note-6) 10 gun Hecla-class bomb vessel launched in 1826
*   [Fury-class sloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fury-class_sloop&action=edit&redlink=1 "Fury-class sloop (page does not exist)") (1813) 12-gun sloop equipped as a bomb vessel
*   [HMS Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Waterloo_/(1818/) "HMS Waterloo (1818)") (1813) 80-gun ship of the line launched in 1818

Ship and Operational _Histories_
================================

We have created this guide to assist in locating information regarding Royal Navy Ships such as their operational histories. Where there may be a charge in accessing a resource we have indicated (£).

See The National Archives (TNA) guides for [Royal Navy operations during the First World War](http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/royal-navy-operations-first-world-war/) and the [Second World War](http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/royal-navy-operations-second-world-war/).

Trace the activities of specific ships using the index in the five volumes covering Naval Operations in _The Official History of the Great War_ and in the 'War at Sea' sections of _The Official History of the Second World War_ at IWM and TNA.

Daily accounts including details of voyages, weather conditions and operations are recorded in the official log books for Royal Navy ships and submarines or Official War Diaries for land-based units serving with the army. See [The National Archives guide to log books](http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/royal-navy-ships-voyages-log-books/).

*   Royal Navy log books for ships ([ADM 53](http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1762)) and submarines ([ADM 173](http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1882)) up to 1987 at TNA
*   Ships' log books for the First World War have been transcribed and are available online via the [Old Weather Project](http://www.naval-history.net/OWShips-LogBooksWW1.htm)
*   Royal Naval Division War Diaries 1914–1919 ([WO 95](http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/results/r?_p=1900&_q=WO+95+Royal+Naval+Division)) are available at TNA and on Ancestry ([Gallipoli and Dardanelles](http://search.ancestry.co.uk/search/db.aspx?dbid=60380) 1914–1916 and [France, Belgium and Germany](https://search.ancestry.co.uk/search/db.aspx?dbid=60779) 1914–1920) (£)

For vessels lost at sea, see [The National Archives guide to ships wrecked or sunk](http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/ships-wrecked-sunk/).

*   Royal Navy ships lost at sea during the First World War – a card index 1914–1919 (ADM 242/6) at [TNA](http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C522009), a list on [Naval History](http://www.naval-history.net/WW1LossesaContents.htm) (free) and with images of the cards on [FindMyPast](http://search.findmypast.co.uk/search-world-Records/ww1-ships-lost-at-sea-1914-1919) (£)
*   [_British vessels lost at sea 1914–1918 and 1939–1945_](https://www.iwm.org.uk/collections/item/object/1500024158) (republished by Patrick Stephens, 1988) – Fascimile reprints of four HMSO official publications: Navy Losses, Merchant Shipping (Losses) published in 1919, Ships of the Royal Navy: statement of losses during the Second World War and British Merchant vessels Lost or damaged by enemy action during Second World War, published in 1947, available at IWM (LBY 88 / 2702) by appointment in our [Research Room](https://www.iwm.org.uk/research/research-facilities). 

Ship histories:

*   IWM has an extensive collection of ship histories, available to search on our [online catalogue](http://www.iwm.org.uk/collections)

To search for ships and locate references, try searching by the name of the:

*   Ship or submarine (for example, 'HMS Wanderer' or 'Wanderer')
*   Operation (for example, 'Operation Neptune' or 'Neptune')
*   Battle (for example, 'Battle of the Java Sea' or 'Java Sea')
*   Theatre of operations (for example, 'Pacific' or 'Persian Gulf')
*   Convoy number (for example, 'HXF 1')
*   Date or month (for example, '27 February 1942' or 'February 1942')

Other things to look for:

2.title: VGhlIE5hdGlvbmFsIEFyY2hpdmVzIC0gSG9tZXBhZ2U=
2.content:
This guide will help you to find Royal Navy log books at The National Archives. These records reveal the location of Royal Navy ships and submarines, wherever they were in the world, and the voyages they took, from around 1669 onwards. Unlike the Army, the Royal Navy did not keep unit war diaries but naval logs are the nearest equivalent to those diaries.

Sometimes other elements of life aboard ship were recorded too, but rarely do logs provide personal information on the officers and crew of a particular ship. Medical officers’ journals (see [section 6](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/royal-navy-ships-voyages-log-books/#6-medical-officers-journals-1785-1963)) are the logs most likely to contain information on individuals.

2\. What information do naval logs contain?
-------------------------------------------

There are various types of naval logs and they do not all contain the same kind of information but most of them reveal:

*   locations of ships
*   movements of ships from one place to another
*   weather that ships encountered
*   signals and orders

Less commonly they can reveal:

*   tasks performed and carried out by ships’ companies
*   disciplinary action carried out on board
*   loss of or damages to stores on board

3\. Search tips
---------------

You can use Discovery, [our catalogue](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/), to search for logs by the name of a ship or submarine and by year. For a more targetted search you can:

*   Go to the [advanced search](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/search/advanced-search) in our catalogue and enter the ship’s or submarine’s name in the keyword field
*   Restrict your search by reference, using any or all of the series references provided in the sections below (for example, ADM 50)

For more tips on searching in the catalogue, use the [Discovery help page](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/discovery-help/).

4\. Officers’ logs 1669-1916
----------------------------

### 4.1 Admirals’ journals 1702-1916

The records in series ADM 50 are the official journals of admirals and officers of acting flag rank, and are of varying forms and completeness.

Consult the [ADM 50 series description](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1759) for information on what the records contain.

Click on the series reference to search for logs in [ADM 50](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1759):

*   by name of admiral up to 1855
*   by name of admiral, station or squadron from 1856 onwards

### 4.2 Masters’ logs 1672-1871

As well as recording a ship’s position, course and the weather, masters’ logs can include details of:

*   punishments issued and carried out
*   duties and tasks carried out by the ship’s hands

Click on the following series references to search for masters’ logs by ship’s name and date:

*   between 1672 and 1840 in [ADM 52](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1761) (read the [ADM 52 series description](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1761) for more information on what the records contain)
*   between 1808 and 1871 in [ADM 54](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1763) (read the [ADM 54 series description](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1763) for more information on what the records contain)

Consult the small collection of miscellaneous logs from between 1648 and 1706, bound into four volumes, in [ADM 7/777](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/browse/C3741196?v=r)\-80.

### 4.3 Captains’ logs 1669-1852

Captains’ logs were compiled from the masters’ logs. The captain added whatever information he thought relevant, or was obliged to give by regulation. The logs can provide a full picture of the daily routine of a naval vessel under sail.

Click on the series reference to search for captains’ logs by ship’s name and date in [ADM 51](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1760).

### 4.4 Lieutenants’ logs

Lieutenants’ logs were derived from the masters’ logs in a similar way to the captains’ logs and are now held by the [National Maritime Museum](https://collections.rmg.co.uk/archive/objects/491964.html "External website - link opens in a new window").

5\. Ships’ logs from 1799 onwards
---------------------------------

The various types of officers’ logs discussed above were, by the mid 19th century, superseded by ships’ logs and these records are held in series ADM 53.

Ships’ captains would inspect the logs weekly and they were then sent to the Admiralty.

Consult the [ADM 53 series description](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1762) for information on what the records contain.

Click on the series reference to search for ships’ logs by ship’s name and date in [ADM 53](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1762).

6\. Medical officers’ journals 1785-1963
----------------------------------------

Medical officers, sometimes referred to as surgeons, on board ship were required to keep a general journal on the health of the ship’s company.

The Navy was always keen to preserve the health of its men and these journals, often written by educated men with acerbic and independent opinions, are usually the most accessible and informative source for the history of a voyage.

Click on the series reference to search for surviving medical officers’ journals in [ADM 101](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/details?Uri=C1810), a record series which also contains other kinds of Admiralty medical journals. Search by:

*   name of ship
*   name of sick or injured person
*   name of sickness, disease or injury (for example, scurvy, consumption, cough, broken leg)
*   other keywords

For a further set of medical journals covering 1858-1867, search [our catalogue](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/) by ship’s name within series [MT 32](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C11081).

The logs contain:

*   details of individuals injured or sick
*   accounts of the medical or surgical treatment of men
*   daily sick lists
*   statistics on diseases
*   comments on the state of health of the crew

7\. Logs and journals of ships of exploration 1757-1904
-------------------------------------------------------

Search and download [captains’ and masters’ logs and private journals kept on voyages of exploration](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/logs-journals-ships-of-exploration-1757-1904/) in our online records pages.

Search [ADM 55](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1764) in [our catalogue](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/) by name of ship and date for log books that are not online.

Search [ADM 51](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1760) in [our catalogue](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/) using “explorations” as your keyword for other log books of ships of exploration.

8\. Submarines’ logs from 1914 onwards
--------------------------------------

Submarine logs were kept by crew members otherwise engaged in steering or depth keeping, and contain many abbreviated references.

Click on the series reference to search for submarines’ logs in [ADM 173](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1882). They record:

*   all wheel, telegraph and depth keeping orders
*   details of battery charges
*   details of torpedo firing
*   navigation information

British Warships in the Age of Sail, 1793-1817: Design, Construction, Careers and Fates

Rif Winfield
Chatham, 2005 - 418页
At the zenith of its power in 1809 the Royal Navy comprised one half of all the warships in the world, the first (and last) time any navy achieved this dominance. Given its importance, it is not surprising that much attention has been lavished on this subject, but among the numerous books on the design, development and technical details of these ships, there is surprisingly little readily available on their careers. Now this gap is comprehensively filled by this superb reference book, outlining the service history of every ship, built, purchased or captured, that fought for the Royal Navy in the great wars of the 1793-1815 era v well over 2000 vessels.

The book is organized by Rate, classification and class, with outline technical and building data, but followed by a concise summary of the careers of each ship in every class. This includes commissioning dates, refit periods, changes of captain, the stations where they served (and when), as well as details of any noteworthy actions in which they took part. It will enable anyone to follow up a casual reference to any warship, and will provide the researcher with a solid core of information on which to base further study. With nothing remotely like it in print, this is a work of the utmost importance to every naval historian and general reader interested in the navy of the Nelsonic era.

6.content:
What are these records?
-----------------------

These records, from series [ADM 196](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/details?Uri=C1905), are the service records of officers who joined the Royal Navy between 1756 and 1931.

They include service records for commissioned officers joining the Navy up to 1917 and warrant officers joining up to 1931.

They also feature the records of Royal Marines officers commissioned between 1793 and 1925.

Commissioned officers included are:

*   admirals (also known as flag officers)
*   commodores
*   captains
*   commanders
*   lieutenants

Warrant officers included are:

*   gunners
*   boatswains
*   carpenters
*   surgeons’ mates
*   armourers
*   sailmakers
*   masters at arms
*   caulkers
*   ropemakers and coopers
*   masters (pre-1808)
*   surgeons (pre-1843)
*   pursers (pre-1843)
*   chaplains (pre-1843)
*   engineers (pre-1847)

How do I search the records?
----------------------------

You can search and download the records in Discovery (£) by filling in the form below.

What information do the records contain?
----------------------------------------

Until the late 19th century these service records tend to be very basic. The majority will contain:

*   an officer’s first name
*   an officer’s rank
*   the names of the ships they served on
*   the dates of entry and discharge from each ship and the total time served
*   they may record an officer’s date of death

From the late 19th century onwards some will also contain:

*   date and place of birth
*   next of kin

[![Image 1: Early service record of Sir Fleetwood Broughton Reynolds Pellew (ADM 196/5)](https://testlb.nationalarchives.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/adm196-pellew1-552x720.jpg)](https://testlb.nationalarchives.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/adm196-pellew1.jpg)

Early service record of Sir Fleetwood Broughton Reynolds Pellew (ADM 196/5)

It is possible for an officer to have multiple service records and in most of these instances we have joined them into one download.

What do the records look like?
------------------------------

Why can’t I find what I’m looking for?
--------------------------------------

If you cannot find a service record the explanation may be that:

*   The officer died or left service before records were systematically kept from the 1840s
*   The officer served with the Royal Naval Reserve or the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve
*   You should be searching for a rating, not an officer; in this case, try [Royal Navy ratings’ service records from 1853 to 1928](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/royal-navy-ratings-service-records-1853-1928/) instead
*   You are searching for an admiral but he is described as a flag officer, another name used for admirals

The record may be held in a different record series instead. Look at records of carpenters or boatswains who enlisted between 1848 and 1912 in [ADM 29/114-115](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/browse/C528437?v=r) and [ADM 29/116-119](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/browse/C528439?v=r). You can find records of engineers who served during 1839-1862 in [ADM 29/105-111](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/browse/C528428?v=r). Try browsing series [ADM 104](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1813) for surgeons’ and assistant surgeons’ service records.

Try searching the [Royal Navy First World War Lives at Sea](https://royalnavyrecordsww1.rmg.co.uk/) database by name, service number and numerous other criteria. As of June 2021, the database contains 32,000 records and is continually being updated. Once completed (scheduled for November 2022), it will contain information relating to all the Royal Navy officers and ratings that served in the First World War. The database is being compiled largely from records held at The National Archives and there is no charge for access. It is a joint project between The National Archives, The National Maritime Museum and the Crew List Index Project with the help of a global team of volunteers.

### Census Records\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&veaction=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Census Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Census Records")\]

Sailors are rarely at home on census night, but when they are any mention of R.N. will alert you to their service in the Royal Navy; the most likely to be found on land are the inactive ones, for example Pensioner RN or _RN Half Pay_. Naval institutions such as schools and hospitals were enumerated of-course and will be found in their relevant district.

Many captains filled out returns for their ships from 1841, and from 1861 members of the Royal Navy (and passengers spending the night on board ship) anywhere in the world were recorded, as were merchant seamen and passengers on ships in British harbours. The returns for ships in British waters are found at the end of the household returns for the registration district in which their next port lay.

Those for the Royal Navy in foreign waters will be found at the end (highest numbers) of the record class, but as these are rarely their hometowns they are difficult to find without union indexes.

If your sailor of any rank was active in 1861 or 1881 there are two invaluable union indexes:

*   A complete index of 120,000 people on ships on the night of 7 April 1861 is on fiche set [FS Library fiche 6025598](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/624063) (8) with a companion fiche showing the ships enumerated on [FS Library fiche 6025599](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/386306) (1).  
    

*   The 1881 surname index for England and Wales has a separate Royal Navy section, which of-course includes R.N. sailors from Scotland and Ireland as well. These can be particularly useful sources for the Irish whose censuses are now missing.

If your ancestor, or his brother, was a sailor in 1861 or 1881 those indexes enable you to find birthplaces.

### Church Records\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&veaction=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Church Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Church Records")\]

Sailors tended to marry and have their children christened in port towns, and the registers of areas of Portsmouth (including Portsea, Landport, Alverstoke and Gosport), and of Plymouth (including East Stonehouse and Stoke Damerel) were huge. It is worth checking the original entries of marriage, christening and infant burial, and not just an index or a transcript, as the sailor’s ship was usually noted in at least some of them. The Hampshire Genealogical Society had special editions of its journal devoted to the port cities of Southampton (May 1999) and Portsmouth (Nov 1999) which make excellent background reading.

A kind of record which should not be overlooked is plaques and monuments in churches commemorating naval and other shipping disasters involving local men.

### Naval Records\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&veaction=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Naval Records") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Naval Records")\]

There are few records prior to the Civil War, but from the time of Restoration in 1660 there is an abundance of records still in existence which shed a great deal of light on seamen’s lives, including such details as what they looked like, what ships or shore bases they served on, where they went, promotions and punishments, and even what they ate! Most navy records were administered by the Admiralty and are thus in ADM classes, but some concerning wages come under the Paymaster General (PMG). In a similar manner to the army, the records of commissioned officers, warrant officers and ratings are different in type and organization.

Records of Royal Navy Commissioned Officers\[[edit](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&veaction=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Records of Royal Navy Commissioned Officers") | [edit source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=England_Royal_Navy_Records_-_International_Institute&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Records of Royal Navy Commissioned Officers")\]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Commissioned Officers were also referred to as _Sea, Fighting_, or _Executive Officers_. Below lists the main available records in date order and brief notes follow; consult Rodger for a more extensive survey.

ADM 76 |- | Passing certificates | 1691-1902 | ADM 6, ADM 13, ADM 107 |- | Service records | 1756-1966 | ADM 196 |- | Black books (misconduct) | 1759-1815 | ADM 12, ADM 11 |- | Navy Lists of various typed  
and biographies | 1782 onwards | Libraries WWI and WWII lists in ADM 177 |- | Leave books | 1783-1847 | ADM 6 |- | Compassionate Fund | 1809-1926 | ADM 22-23, PMG 18 |- | Survey Returns | 1817-51 | ADM 9, ADM 6, ADM 11 |- | Widows Claims for Back Pay | 1830-1860 | ADM 45 |- | Widows Pensions | 1836-1929 | PMG 19 |- | Medal recommendations | 1854-1960s | ADM 1, ADM 116, ADM 171 |- | Exam results | 1876-1957 | ADM 203 |- | Post WWI records | 1923-1939 | Anyone can apply to Min of Defence, CS(R)2e |- | WWII onwards | 1939 to date | Next of kin can apply to HMS Centurion |}

_**Annual Lists**_  
The best place to start looking for an officer is in one of the several annual lists that record their names, rank, ship and date of commission, examples being:

*   _Navy List,_ which started as _Steel’s Navy List_ in 1782, names all commissioned officers including masters, pursers, surgeons, chaplains, yard officers, coast guardsmen and reservists. A copy of the 1795 list is on [FS Library film 0496423](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/265930) (item 2) and the volumes from 1851 to 1935 are [on 18 FS Library films starting at film 0918928](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/61246), whilst fiche copies of 1821, 1851 and 1920 can be purchased from M.M. Publications.  
    

*   _Whitaker’s Naval and Military Directory and Indian Army List_ is available on [FS Library film 1656909](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/421385) and lists both officers and ships.

Many other such lists may be found in the FamilySearch Catalog under GREAT BRITAIN -MILITARY RECORDS-NAVY as well as BIOGRAPHY and OFFICIALS AND EMPLOYEES, for example Admiralty Officials 1660-1870 as book 942 N2o v.4

There are several printed _biographies of naval officers_:

*   _Commissioned Sea Officers of the Royal Navy 1660-1815_ by Syrett and Dinardo is [on two FS Library films, Vols I and II on film 0908026](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/281371), III on [FS Library film 0908027](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/281371).   
    

*   _Marshall’s Naval Biography_ 1760-1823.   
    

*   Charnock’s _Biographica Navalis_ 1660-1794.   
    

*   _British Naval Officers_ is a manuscript of 80 high ranking naval officers of the 1720-1820 period on [FS Library film 0990317](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/412707) item 6.   
    

*   _O’Byrne’s Naval Biographical Dictionary_ based on the 1845 Navy List of all 5,000 living officers is on [FS Library film 0845144 or fiche 6091076](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/244746) (15). A fiche reprint is also available from M.M. Publications.

|- | **DASHWOOD. (Captain, in 1818. F-P., 15; H-P., 33)** WILLIAM BATEMAN DASHWOOD WAS BORN 1 Sep 1790. This officer entered the Navy 3 Aug 1799 as Fst.-cl. Vol., on board the DEFIANCE 74, Caps Thos Revell Shivers and Rich. Retallick, flag-ship afterwards of rear-Admiral Thos Graves, under whom he served at the battle of Copenhagen 2 April 1801. On 22 June 1802 he became Midshipman of the ISIS 50, bearing the flag in succession of the late Lord Gambier, of Sir Edw Thornbrough, and of Sir Erasmus Gower, at Newfoundland, where he continued until Feb 1805; after which he joined, consecutively, the POMONE 44, Capt W, Grenville Lobb, off Lisbon, CAPTAIN 74, Capt Geo Cockburn, at Spithead, and MODESTE 36, Capt Geo Elliott. On 15 Aug 1807, being then in the East Indies, Mr. Dashwood was appointed Acting-Lieutenant of the CULLODEN 74, flag-ship of Sir Edw Pellew, from which we find him officially promoted, 28 Jan 1808, into his former ship, the MODESTE. Invaliding home in July 1809 he next, on 12 June 1810, joined the ATLAS 74, Capt Jas Sanders, and was for some time employed in the gun-boat service at the siege of Cadiz. Prior to his appointment, as First-Lieutenant, to the ACTIVE of 46 guns, Capt Jas Alex Gordon, which took place in Oct 1811, Mr Dashwood further served for a few months with Capt Clephane, on board the CUMBERLAND and AJAZ 74’s. On 29 Nov in the latter year, he shared in a hard-fought action of an hour and forty minutes, which, in rendering the ACTIVE captor of _La Pomone_, of 44 guns and 332 men, 50 of whom were killed and wounded, cost her a loss of 8 killed and 27 wounded; and on that occasion he had the misfortune to have his right arm shot off, a few minutes after the disablement of Capt Gordon, who lost a leg. Being promoted to the rank of commander 19 May 1812, and appointed, 23 July 1813, to the SNAP 16, Capt Dashwood now cruized off the coast of France, where on 1 Nov, he fell in with five privateer luggers, one of which, _Le Lion_¸ of 16 guns and 69 men, he brought to close action, and in ten minutes captured. On 15 Nov 1814, he removed to the PROMETHEUS sloop, and after hovering about the Bay of Biscay for some time in the summer of 1815, with a view to the interception of Napoleon Buonaparte, sailed for the Mediterranean; on which station he assisted at the bombardment of Algiers 27 Aug 1816. Previously to that event he had succeeded in brining away, disguised as midshipmen, the wife and daughter of the British Consul, Mr M’Donell. Capt Dashwood, who paid the PROMETHEUS off in Nov 1816, was subsequently appointed to the Acting command, 23 July 1818 of the CREOLE 36, fitting for South America, where he attained Post-rank, 21 Oct following, in the AMPHION 32. He went on half-pay in May 1819; and accepted the Retirement 1 Oct 1846. Capt Dashwood is Senior of 1818. In consideration of his wound he enjoys a pension of 200l. He married, 17 April 1820, Louisa Henrietta, only daughter of Fred. Bode Esq. by whom he has issue.

AGENTS—Hallett and Robinson.

Not sure? Search 10 years either side

Search

![Image 1: Discover Hero image](https://d3nd02ak4v4ued.cloudfront.net/image-proxy/fn:discover_hero_image_main_94d47ae963png.png/f:webp/rs:fit:400/czM6Ly9wYXlsb2FkLWNtcy1wcm9kdWN0aW9uL2Rpc2NvdmVyX2hlcm9faW1hZ2VfbWFpbl85NGQ0N2FlOTYzcG5nLnBuZw==)

![Image 2: Discover learn about image](https://d3nd02ak4v4ued.cloudfront.net/image-proxy/fn:discover_learn_about_image_136191e0b01png.png/f:webp/rs:fit/czM6Ly9wYXlsb2FkLWNtcy1wcm9kdWN0aW9uL2Rpc2NvdmVyX2xlYXJuX2Fib3V0X2ltYWdlXzEzNjE5MWUwYjAxcG5nLnBuZw==)

Search our genealogy records
----------------------------

This collection of muster rolls is an excellent resource for genealogists to find seafaring ancestors in the Royal Navy before service records began in 1853. Easily search the records by name. The records come exclusively from The National Archives and cover the years 1739 to 1861.

Learn about these records
-------------------------

What can these records tell me?keyboard\_arrow\_down

Each result will provide you with an image of the original record from The National Archives and a transcript of the vital information. The details of each transcript can vary depending on the amount of information recorded in the original document. You may find a combination of the following information:

*   Name
*   Sex
*   Birth year
*   Birth parish
*   Birth county
*   Birth country
*   Enlistment year – shown on the image as appearance date
*   Muster year
*   Muster date
*   Ship name
*   Location
*   Record type
*   Archive
*   Series and reference
*   Series description

**Images**

The images will provide you with further detail about your ancestor such as the date, place, and reason for your ancestor’s discharge. Many of the muster rolls recorded your ancestor’s rank or rating. Often the ratings were abbreviated, for example AB was used for an able-bodied seaman.

The ADM 38 series records are the most abundant of the three series represented in this collection for information about your ancestor. Almost every entry recorded a physical description of your ancestor, his marital status, whether or not he had been vaccinated for smallpox, and the names of previous ships your ancestor served on.

Discover more about these recordskeyboard\_arrow\_down

The muster rolls and a small number of pay lists found in **British Royal Navy, Ships’ Musters** are an excellent resource for anyone searching for an ancestor in the navy before 1853. Before 1853, men joined the navy on a short-term basis and did not permanently enlist. This meant that each sailor did not have his own service record. Permanent or continuous service in the Royal Navy began after 1853. In other cases, men were conscripted for short service or during times of war, and men serving on captured ships could be impressed into the navy and forced to work. The muster roll books of the Royal Navy recorded the names of every person present on board a ship. The books were kept on an 8-week basis. They were used for accounting and administrative reasons.

The original records are retained by The National Archives (TNA) in England. Before digitisation, you would have had to visit TNA and trawl through the numerous muster rolls to try to find your ancestor’s name. Now that Findmypast has digitised the records, you can search them easily by name, birth place, and ship name. The records are from TNA’s ADM 36, ADM 37, and ADM 38 series. The **British Royal Navy, Ships’ Musters** is not inclusive of every muster roll found within those series from the archives.

You can find the muster rolls for ships used during wars with France, Spain, and America, as well as those employed through the Napoleonic Wars. Some defended against the invasion of the ‘Young Pretender’, Charles Edward Stuart, in 1745, and others surrendered to the American forces at the Battle of Yorktown in 1781. You can also discover the muster roll from Lord Nelson’s _HMS Victory_ from August to October of 1805, only weeks before the Royal Navy’s greatest achievement at the Battle of Trafalgar.

The records also include almost 1,000 entries for ‘Widow’s Men’. You can find these records by searching for Widow’s Men or Widow in the keyword field. Widow’s men were listed on the ship’s muster roll to ensure that money was allocated for the widows of men who had died while in service. An act of Parliament allowed the cost of pay for one able-bodied seaman for every one hundred on board to be set aside for widows. This practice ended in 1823.

Contents
--------

*   [1\. Why use this guide?](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/ships-wrecked-sunk/#1-why-use-this-guide)
*   [2\. How to conduct a search at The National Archives](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/ships-wrecked-sunk/#2-how-to-conduct-a-search-at-the-national-archives)
*   [3\. Additional records and publications of First World War losses](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/ships-wrecked-sunk/#3-additional-records-and-publications-of-first-world-war-losses)
*   [4\. Additional records and publications of Second World War losses](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/ships-wrecked-sunk/#4-additional-records-and-publications-of-second-world-war-losses)
*   [5\. Beyond The National Archives: where else to look for information and records](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/ships-wrecked-sunk/#5-beyond-the-national-archives-where-else-to-look-for-information-and-records)
*   [6\. Further reading](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/ships-wrecked-sunk/#6-further-reading)

1\. Why use this guide?
-----------------------

Use this guide for advice on how to find records at The National Archives, and to a lesser extent in other archives, of Royal Navy shipwrecks. The records covered include those that document the complete loss of ships through sinking as well as those lost to damage, whether as part of a military conflict, a result of natural disaster or any other accident. Some of the records will allow you simply to establish that a ship sunk or was wrecked, others can provide more detail, such as the circumstances of the disaster or incident and the number on board who died, if any.

You can also consult our guide to [births, marriages and deaths at sea](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/birth-marriage-death-sea-or-abroad/).

2\. How to conduct a search at The National Archives
----------------------------------------------------

A search in The National Archives’ records will almost certainly require a [visit to our reading rooms in Kew](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/about/visit-us/) where you can consult library books and original documents. Most of the records we hold for lost ships are not available to download or view online but you can, however, make a start online by searching [our catalogue](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/) (see Step 2, below).

We recommend you follow these steps, in the order shown, when searching for records of the loss or damage to a specific ship:

### Step 1: Consult the Royal Navy Lost List and/or lists in published books

The Royal Navy Loss List is a searchable database on the [Maritime Archaeology Sea Trust](https://thisismast.org/research/royal-navy-loss-list.html) website. It covers all vessels recorded as sunk or destroyed in service from 1512-2004 but does not include vessels captured by the enemy or that suffered loss of life but which did not sink. The purpose of the list was to record losses which are likely to have resulted in material remains on the sea floor.

There are a number of alternative lists in printed publications, many available at The National Archives library, and they are likely to be the easiest way of establishing the date and circumstances of the loss, if they are known, and will equip you with vital facts in your search for primary sources – or may remove the need to consult original documents altogether.

The following books are available at our library in Kew, as are those listed for the First and Second World Wars in the subsequent sections of this guide. They are the best place to start on a visit to our reading rooms.

*   Larn, R and Larn, B, [Shipwreck Index of the British Isles](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=3396) (Lloyd’s Register of Shipping, 1995-2002). These six volumes are the most comprehensive listing of wrecks in UK coastal areas up to the end of the 20th century. Organised by county and date, with a ship name index, among the details provided with each listing are the name of the captain, the number of crew on board and lost, if any, and the origin and intended destination of the voyage.
*   Gosset, W P, [The Lost Ships of the Royal Navy, 1793-1900](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=37711) (Mansell Publishing, 1986). Contains a ship name index and a geographical index listing ships lost by region.
*   Hepper, D J, [British Warship Losses in the Age of Sail, 1650-1859](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=25628) (Jean Boudriot Publications, 1994). Chronological list with details of the circumstances of the loss.
*   Hocking, C, [Dictionary of Disasters at Sea during the Age of Steam, 1824-1962](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=35572) (Lloyd’s Register of Shipping, 1969). Two volumes listing ships in alphabetical order with a short description of the disaster and the date, among other details. Includes Royal Navy and  merchant ships.
*   Hooke, N, [Modern Shipping Disasters, 1963-1987](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=10) (Lloyds of London Press, 1989). A sequel to Hocking’s Dictionary of Disasters at Sea, presented in the same format.
*   Marx, R, [Shipwrecks of the Western Hemisphere, 1492-1825](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=22776), (David Mckay Co, 1975). Covering shipwrecks in the Caribbean and all over the Americas, several thousand losses are listed in date order and briefly described. The book covers ships of all types and includes a ship name index.
*   Grocott, T, [Shipwrecks of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Eras](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=12232) (Caxton, 2002). Contemporary newspaper accounts of both merchant and military ships wrecked. Organised by date but with a ship name index.

### Step 2: Search the catalogue with ship’s name and one other search term

Though the records of ships losses are not always identified by the ships’ names in our online catalogue, it is worth trying to locate those that are at an early stage of your search.

Search [our catalogue](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/) using the name of the ship (omitting HMS as it is not always used in catalogue descriptions) plus one of the following words:

*   sunk
*   sinking
*   loss
*   wreck/wrecked
*   torpedo/torpedoing/torpedoed
*   damage
*   attack

To target the records of the Admiralty, the body that administered the Royal Navy, use the [advanced search](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/advanced-search) of our catalogue and use the references fields to restrict your search to reference ADM.

### Step 3: Consult the ship’s log, if it survives

We hold large numbers of Royal Navy ships’ logs from the 1660s onwards, though not all survive. The log book may give the position of the sinking, though the ship may have been wrecked because its officers did not know where they were. However, logbooks were often lost with the ship and in these instances you should turn to the logs of any other ships which sailed in company with the lost ship.

To search for logs, which are arranged alphabetically by ships’ names, click on the following series links and search by ship’s name or, for Masters’ logs, by the name of the officer who wrote the log:

*   Captains’ logs, 1669-1853, in [ADM 51](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1760)
*   Masters’ logs, 1672-1840, in [ADM 52](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1761)
*   Log books maintained by the Officer of the Watch, 1799-2007, in [ADM 53](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1762)
*   Supplementary ships’ logs, 1808-1871, in [ADM 54](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1763)

### Step 4: Search for a courts martial record, if there was an inquiry

The loss of Royal Navy ships usually resulted in an inquiry, with the captain or surviving officers sometimes court martialled, though this was far less likely if the ship was lost to enemy action or if none of the officers survived.

These records can be the most detailed narratives of a loss available, although, as the court’s purpose was to establish the circumstances of the loss and to apportion any blame, it did not necessarily take an interest in the exact position of the wreck.

Click on the following series links to search each series by year and by words such as ‘loss’, ‘sinking’ or ‘grounding’ plus the name of a ship for:

*   1892-1951 in [ADM 178](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1887)
*   1890-1965 in [ADM 156](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1865)
*   1660-1976 in [ADM 1](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1710) (most are indexed in [The Lost Ships of the Royal Navy, 1793-1900](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=37711)) – to search in this series you will need to include ‘courts martial’ as one of your search terms

### Step 5: Search through Admiralty and Navy Board correspondence and case files

There are many records which were not created specifically to record losses but which do, nonetheless, either formally record losses or contain incidental references to them. Using these records for details of a wreck is bound to be quite time consuming and should be considered a last resort if you have followed the steps above and still need information. The principal records to search through are:

*   Reports from flag officers and captains on the loss of ships under their command from about 1698 onward in [ADM 1](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C1710). See our guidance on [How to use ADM 12 to locate items in ADM 1](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/naval-correspondence-adm12-indexes-and-digests/).
*   Case files created by the Admiralty Record Office, 1852-1965, in [ADM 116](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1825).
*   Letters sent to the Navy Board, or by that board to the Admiralty in [ADM 106](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1815), which occasionally deal with wrecks, particularly those which occurred in the vicinity of dockyard ports or where salvage was attempted. We also hold digests, summarising contents of each letter or paper, for 1822 to 1832 in [ADM 106/2153 to 2177](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/browse/r/r/C4110029).
*   The Admiralty Digest in  [ADM 12](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1721), which provides a name and subject index from 1793 onward. See our guidance on [How to use ADM 12](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/naval-correspondence-adm12-indexes-and-digests/) to get the most from this series and the various series that it indexes.

3\. Additional records and publications of First World War losses
-----------------------------------------------------------------

You can find records of First World War losses by following the steps in section 2 but in this section we present publications and records focussed specifically on the war.

### Books

The following publication is available at our library in Kew and is the best place to start when conducting a search at The National Archives:

*   HMSO, [British Vessels Lost at Sea 1914-1918 and 1939-1945](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=2686) (Patrick Stephens, 1988)

### Lists

A card index of ships lost between 1914 and 1919 in [ADM 242/6](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C522009).

### Narrative accounts

Search with a ship’s name and the word ‘loss’, ‘torpedoing’ ‘sinking’ (or any of the other keywords suggested at Step 2 in section 2 of this guide) to search the records used to compile the Official History of the First World War held in [ADM 137](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1846). The series includes hundreds of reports on the losses of individual ships, found between [ADM 137/3089 and ADM 137/3832](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/browse/r/r/C4114760).

4\. Additional records and publications of Second World War losses
------------------------------------------------------------------

You can find records of Second World War losses by following the steps in section 2 but in this section we present publications and records focussed specifically on the war.

### Books

The following books are available at our library in Kew and are the best place to start when conducting a search at The National Archives:

*   HMSO, [British Vessels Lost at Sea 1914-1918 and 1939-1945](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=2686) (Patrick Stephens, 1988)
*   Brown, D, [Warship Losses of World War Two](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=25468) (Arms & Armour Press, 1990)
*   Lenton, H T & Colledge, J J, [Warships of World War Two](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=37709) (Ian Allan Publishing, 1973)
*   Morgan, D & Taylor, B, [U-Boat Attack Logs: A Complete Record of the Warship Sinkings From Original Sources 1939-1945](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=59160) (Seaforth Publishing, 2012)
*   Rohwer, J, [Axis Submarine Successes 1939-1945](https://tna.koha-ptfs.co.uk/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=27830) (Patrick Stephens Ltd, 1993)

### Lists

Search the lists of Royal Navy ships lost in the war held in [ADM 213/578](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C518563).

### Narrative accounts

The records used to compile the Official History of the Second World War are held in [ADM 199](https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C1908) and include reports of ships lost during the war. Search the series with a ship’s name and the terms ‘loss’, ‘ships lost’, ‘torpedoing’ ‘sinking’ or any of the other keywords suggested at Step 2 in section 2 of this guide.

5\. Beyond The National Archives: where else to look for information and records
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Newspaper reports

The most comprehensive source for archived newspapers is the [British Newspaper Archive](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/). Local libraries may provide access to online versions of national newspapers, including The Times Archive, also available online in our reading rooms.

As well as the [British Newspaper Archive](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/), the British Library holds the largest readily accessible collection of printed Admiralty charts in its [Map Library](https://www.bl.uk/subjects/maps). Sea charts may be useful in establishing the location of a wreck, but usually not in identifying it. See our [guide to sea charts](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/sea-charts/) for more information.

### UK Parliamentary Papers

The Admiralty Register of Wrecks is found in [Proquest UK Parliamentary Papers](https://parlipapers.proquest.com/parlipapers/search/basic/hcppbasicsearch). This is a subscription website you can access on The National Archives’ computers by visiting us at Kew. You may also be able to access it via a large reference library such as a university library.

### UK Hydrographic Office

A comprehensive database of wrecks containing over 60,000 records, of which approximately 20,000 are for named vessels, is maintained by the [UK Hydrographic Office](https://www.ukho.gov.uk/Pages/home.aspx). Though focussed mainly on UK territorial waters the database includes information on a small number of wrecks in other areas. The same office holds an extensive collection of British Admiralty Charts and other hydrographic charts.

6\. Further reading
-------------------

Huntress, K, Checklist of Narratives of Shipwrecks & Disasters at Sea to 1860 (Iowa State University Press, 1979) – a guide to contemporary accounts of losses

Pickford, N, The Atlas of Shipwreck & Treasure (London, Dorling Kindersley, 1994)

Rohwer, J, Allied Submarine Attacks of World War Two: European Theatre of Operations 1939-45 (Greenhill, 1997)
